title: After Studying Abroad at Tulane University
paragraphs: This time I experienced a two-month hospital clerkship at Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans, in the United States. The greatest reason I entered Nagoya University was that I was attracted by the exchange program, so I am very glad that I was able to complete the two months of training safely this time. I chose America not only to improve my English but also because I wanted to broaden my horizons by meeting diverse people from all over the world with various backgrounds, wanted to see the differences from Japanese medical care, and wanted to see how American medical students work. New Orleans is famous as a city of jazz and alcohol, and wanting to enjoy its culture was also one of the reasons.

Before starting the local clerkship, there was much hardship, not only preparing for the clerkship but also finding that the dispatch period had been halved from the plan, that the department I wanted was not approved, and that we did not have the right to view charts. Thinking that since it was a precious opportunity we should do what we could and have no regrets, each time a problem arose we did everything within our power, such as negotiating locally. As a result, some parts did not go as I wished, but I think it became a very good experience, including the hardships.

In the hospital clerkship I was allowed to rotate for two weeks each through pulmonology, obstetrics and gynecology, and cardiology. In the first, pulmonology, I was assigned to the ICU team and faced the first day nervously. When I got there, everyone was busy with their own work and there was no one to talk to continuously, so I tried to speak up on my own as much as possible, so as not to become part of the furniture, and made an effort to actively ask questions about the patients. However, it was difficult to keep up with the fast-paced English discussions, and I keenly felt my lack of ability. Even so, in the second week I was allowed to take charge of one patient, gave a presentation to the team, and became able to join the discussion somewhat.

In obstetrics and gynecology, I rotated through obstetrics and gynecology for one week each. Many third-year medical students were rotating, and they, like the residents, went on rounds every morning, wrote charts, gave presentations and thought out treatment policy, starting this work before 6 a.m., and I was stunned by the difference from Japanese students. I was also allowed to observe deliveries and take part in cesarean sections, and I was moved that the joy and emotion when a baby is born are the same in any country. Almost all deliveries were painless deliveries, and I felt cultural differences, for example when Muslim patients refused male doctors and it became a problem.

In the last department, cardiology, I was assigned to the consult team. Every time a cardiology consult came from another department, I did the interview and physical examination, presented to the fellow, and went to see the patient together, and that was how my days went. There were many common diseases such as heart failure and angina, which was educational, and when there were no consults I observed cardiac catheterisation and the ER, so I think I spent meaningful time.

Outside the clerkship, I went out drinking on weekends with students I met there, and in April a festival was held every weekend, so I took part. I was also able to travel around America using my vacation, and I lived very fulfilling days.

Having spent two months in New Orleans, I talked every day with people of various backgrounds, such as African American, Indian, Chinese and white, and each day was stimulating. Also, unlike Japan, America is a multiethnic country, and I felt the existence of an unbridgeable gap between rich and poor and the dilemma of the healthcare system that results from it. I was able to live a life completely different from Japan, and I think my world broadened greatly.

I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to 西尾-san, Dr. 長谷川 and the other doctors of the International Collaboration Office, who supported this study abroad, my family, and the friends who spent time together with me at Tulane. Thank you.
